 Well, it's official: there are two new kids on the block. The new MacBook Pro M6 and the MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen are finally here. If you've been waiting to upgrade, or are looking to pick up your first-ever MacBook, now's the time to do it. Pre-orders are live , and we've even found a trick to help you save up to $1,400 on the OLED model .
 As someone who owns a MacBook and uses one for work, and coincidentally tests the latest and greatest peripherals, I know that your setup isn't complete until you buy the right accessories. I couldn't get on with my work without my trusty mouse, keyboard, monitor, and other gadgets.
 Whether you're after a new mechanical keyboard or even a touch-sensitive one whose keycaps double as a trackpad, a pair of earbuds, or need a USB-C dock for more connectivity, I've got you covered. I've rounded up what I believe are the best accessories (and gadgets) to make the most of your new MacBook Pro M6 or OLED.
 New MacBook Pro pre-orders 
 OLED touchscreen
 MacBook Pro OLED 14-inch: $2,899 at Apple The MacBook Pro OLED is one of the biggest MacBook releases in recent years. It can be configured with an M5 Pro (from $2,899) or M5 Max (from $4,499) CPU and packs a 14.2-inch PROLED XDR touchscreen display with 3024 x 1986 resolution, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB SSD. You also get three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports, HDMI port, and an SDXC slot. The laptop will be available on November 6. 
 View Deal 
 M6 chip
 MacBook Pro M6 14-inch: $1,999 at Amazon Power users looking for a boost in performance should opt for the new 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro. This powerful laptop sports Apple's M6 chip for blazing-fast performance at home or on the go.
 View Deal 
 Monitor 
 27-inch
 Apple Studio Display: was $1,569 now $1,519 at BHPhoto There's no better monitor for your new MacBook Pro than the first-party Apple Studio Display, thanks to its excellent 12MP ultra-wide camera, fantastic six-speaker setup and gorgeous 27-inch 5K screen. It's bright and delivers accurate (and stunning) colors, too.
 Read our full Apple Studio Display review . 
 View Deal 
 27-inch
 BenQ MA270S: $999 at benq.com If you don't mind a third-party display, I can't recommend the BenQ MA270S enough. It's cheaper than the Apple Studio Display and boasts wide color coverage and excellent accuracy, making it a great choice for creatives, and it comes with an Apple-like app for customization. There’s no shortage of ports, and the Nano Gloss 5K panel is a sight to behold.
 Read my full BenQ MA270S review . 
 View Deal 
 40-inch
 Alogic Edge 5K: $1,699 at Adorama If you want more screen real estate, the Alogic Edge 40-inch 5K is an excellent choice. Boasting great color coverage and accuracy, and hosting a plethora of ports for Mac users, this monitor offers everything you could ask for. Available in Silver and Space Gray, it’ll fit right into your existing Mac-first setup, too.
 Read my full Alogic Edge 5K review . 
 View Deal 
 Keyboard 
 Touch-sensitive
 Clevetura S: $199 at Amazon The Clevetura S is an outstanding travel-friendly keyboard with touch-sensitive keycaps that turn it into a highly effective and responsive trackpad with MacBook gestures, negating the need for a separate mouse. Its scissor switches are great to type on, too.
 Read my full Clevetura S review . 
 View Deal 
 100% layout
 Keychron K10 Max: $119 at Amazon The K10 Max is a fantastic iteration of the tried-and-true Keychron formula, offering additional sound dampening, a refined mounting system, and high-performance Super Switches. A deep, thick sound and responsive keystrokes make this a great gaming option, too. It comes with macOS keycaps, making it a solid choice for Apple users.
 Read our full Keychron K10 Max review . 
 View Deal 
 75% layout
 Epomaker Glyph: was $139 now $132 at Amazon Want a keyboard that looks a bit different? The typewriter-like Epomaker Glyph (featuring macOS keycaps) is a wonderful, whimsical addition to any setup. It puts the joy back into typing. The keyboard sports a charming typewriter-like design with dual screens and customizable RGB lighting, and build quality is solid.
 Read my full Epomaker Glyph review . 
 View Deal 
 Mouse 
 Touch-sensitive
 Apple Magic Mouse (USB-C): $79 at BHPhoto There's no better mouse for the MacBook other than the Apple Magic Mouse (as long as you don't mind the very flat design). It features a Multi-Touch surface that allows you to perform gestures, and the mouse can last up to a month between charges. This model features a USB-C port. On the bottom.
 View Deal 
 Ergonomic
 BenQ INFTYLAB M Mouse PS01: $119 at BHPhoto If you want an ergonomic mouse with buttons that toggle macOS shortcuts, try the BenQ INFTYLAB M Mouse PS01. It features dual scrolling wheels, smooth tracking, and you can assign macOS gestures to its buttons. User-friendly companion software makes customization easy, too.
 Read my full BenQ INFTYLAB M Mouse PS01 review . 
 View Deal 
 Gaming
 Corsair M75 (Mac): $129 at Apple Given how powerful both the MacBook Pro M6 and OLED sound, I won't be surprised if they're great for gaming. The Corsair M75 (Mac) is a superb gaming mouse designed for macOS. This minimalist-looking mouse features 26,000 DPI sensitivity that you can change on the fly, making it suitable for all kinds of gaming titles. It’s very comfortable to use for long hours.
 Read my full Corsair M75 (Mac) review . 
 View Deal 
 Dock 
 Desk-made
 UGREEN 8-in-1 Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station: was $249 now $169 at Amazon The UGREEN 8-in-1 Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station is a must-have for those who have a desk setup. It's equipped with three Thunderbolt 4 ports (40Gbps, 15W), three USB-A ports (10Gbps), a gigabit ethernet port, and a 140W DC power port. It's great for creatives and professionals who need high transfer speeds.
 View Deal 
 Portable
 Anker 8-in-1 USB-C Hub: $53 at Amazon I couldn't live without my portable USB-C hub. The Anker 8-in-1 USB-C Hub is ideal for those on the move. It features multiple USB-C and USB-A ports, as well as HDMI 4K/60Hz ports for streaming and mirroring content. There are also two SD and microSD card slots — perfect for photographers and videographers.
 View Deal 
 Stand 
 Fixed, non-adjustable
 Twelve South Curve Stand: $59 at Apple The Twelve South Curve Stand sports a modern and minimal design that complements and enhances your MacBook and workspace. It raises your screen off the desk for improved ergonomics and airflow.
 View Deal 
 Adjustable
 Twelve South Curve Flex Stand: $79 at Apple The Twelve South Curve Flex Stand elevates your MacBook up to 22 inches and adjusts your keyboard angle from zero to 45°, resulting in a more ergonomic and comfortable viewing and typing experience. It folds flat so you can take it with you when you travel.
 View Deal 
 Earbuds 
 Open-ear
 Apple AirPods 5: $129 at Best Buy If you have an existing Apple ecosystem (iPhone, iPad, MacBook, etc.), the Apple AirPods 5 are an excellent choice. Starting from just $124, these affordable earbuds are the ideal model those on a budget. While the battery life is abysmal, the sound quality, comfort, fit, smart features, and ANC make up for it for casual users.
 Read our full Apple AirPods 5 review . 
 View Deal 
 Sealed in-ear
 Apple AirPods 3 Pro: was $249 now $199 at Amazon If you need AirPods that don't skimp on features, the AirPods Pro 3 are the ones for you. They pack useful features like heart rate monitor and Live Translation. The fit is fantastic and comfortable, and there's plenty of battery to keep them going for long listening sessions.
 Read our full Apple AirPods Pro 3 review . 
 View Deal 
 Over-ear
 Apple AirPods Max 2: was $549 now $449 at Amazon Stuffed full of AirPods Pro-esque features like Head Gestures, Live Translation, Camera Remote, and improved Siri integration, the AirPods Max 2 pack lots of smart tech features alongside sound that's rich, complex, and most importantly, fun.
 Read our full Apple AirPods Max 2 review . 
 View Deal 
 Sleeve 
 14-inch or 16-inch
 TomToc 360 Protective Sleeve: $42 at Amazon The TomToc 360 Protective Sleeve is a must-have for those who want to protect their new MacBook Pro M6 or OLED when they're traveling. With four corner protectors, resilient edges, high-density padding, and water-resistant fabric, it protects your laptop from inevitable bumps, scratches and water spills. It also has two separate compartments with several small pockets and a strap for an AirTag or key.
 View Deal 
 14-inch or 16-inch
 Rains Laptop Portfolio: $80 at Apple If you want a more low-key sleeve, the Rains Laptop Portfolio waterproof sleeve is sleek and good-looking. It features a flap closure fastened with concealed magnetic straps, and it's made of durable and smooth PU fabric.
 View Deal

 You've got yourself a MacBook Pro, and you're here to find a display that will act as the perfect companion for your desk setup. Well, after connecting Apple's Pro laptop to the latest screens that land on our desks, we've done the testing and found the best monitors for MacBook Pro.
 Apple's 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros already come equipped with amazing Liquid Retina XDR displays, but to extend your workspace with monitors that match the rich, colorful visuals and high pixel density those screens offer raises the bar for your setup. That's why my team of experts and I have done extensive hands-on testing for picture quality, color accuracy, connectivity and more for each monitor to help you find the right fit for your desk.
 Right now, we highly recommend the Philips 27E3U7903 as the best monitor for MacBook Pro for most, as this 5K beauty ticks all the right boxes and is far less expensive than Apple's Studio Display (even though that is still a great choice). We've got more choices to put on your radar, so if you're ready to give your MacBook Pro the monitor it deserves, our guide will point you in the right direction.
 Looking for other displays from Apple's lineup of Macs? Check out our guides on the best monitors for Mac mini and the best monitors for Mac Studio , too.

 1. Philips 27E3U7903 
 The best monitor for your MacBook Pro around
 Our expert review:
 Specifications
 Screen size: 27 inches 
 Resolution: 5120 x 2880 
 Brightness: 500 nits SDR, 600 nits HDR 
 Color gamut: 99% DCI-P3 
 Connectivity: 1x HDMI 2.1, 1x Thunderbolt 4 with 96W PD upstream, 1x Thunderbolt 4 downstream,1x USB-C upstream, 1x USB-C downstream, 2x USB-A, headphone out

 Reasons to buy
 + 5K pixel density
 + Outstanding connectivity
 + Punchy IPS panel
 Reasons to avoid
 - Very expensive
 - Not a huge subjective upgrade over 4K
 - Calibration could be a bit better
 The Philips 27E3U7903 takes the crown as our top pick for MacBook Pro users who want a monitor that nails modern connectivity and delivers a true high-res experience without the Apple tax. In our testing, we found it needs to be excellent across the board to justify its premium price, and the combination of practical features and 5K clarity gets it most of the way there.
 Connectivity is where the 27E3U7903 shines. With HDMI 2.1, a Thunderbolt 4 port delivering 96W of Power Delivery (enough to fully charge a MacBook Pro), plus additional Thunderbolt, USB-C, and USB-A ports, it handles single-cable docking, peripheral charging, and daisy chaining with ease. We found the built-in KVM switch and multi-port options made switching between devices and tidying up desk clutter genuinely seamless.
 On the visual front, you’re getting a 5K (5120 x 2880) panel using IPS Black tech, meaning crisp, retina-style sharpness for macOS, vibrant colors, and a punchy backlight. In hands-on use, the panel’s vibrancy and power stood out, making it suitable for everything from spreadsheets to creative work, even if it won’t quite match Apple on calibration out of the box.
 Yes, the Apple Studio Display still wins for build quality and Mac integration, but the Philips matches its resolution and undercuts it on price. So you aren’t paying for the logo.
 If you’re looking for a premium-feeling, high-resolution monitor that offers practical one-cable MacBook Pro docking, the 27E3U7903 is a strong choice. You’ll give up some of Apple’s design polish and factory calibration, but for most users after ports, clarity, and versatility, it’s the best all-rounder we’ve tested.

 + Very affordable
 + Versatile ergonomics

 Reasons to avoid
 - No cable management
 - Not all that bright
 - No KVM
 The BenQ GW2486TC Eye-Care Monitor is as budget-friendly as it gets for MacBook Pro users who just want a reliable desktop screen with a single-cable USB-C connection.
 You get 65W USB-C power delivery (enough for lighter MacBooks and most workdays), a 24-inch 1080p IPS panel, and a measured 99% sRGB color coverage. That simple yet effective combination delivers sharp enough text and reasonably accurate colors for routine tasks and light creative work.
 We used this monitor daily for a month, pairing it with various laptops and running through everything from spreadsheets to streaming media, and it made for a great screen companion. For one, the stand offers 130mm of height adjustment, 45-degree swivel, and 90-degree pivot, so it’s easy to dial in a comfortable setup. Secondly, the OSD menu is straightforward, and those eye-care modes are a genuine plus for long sessions, especially if your workday stretches late.
 Of course, you’re making clear trade-offs versus pricier options. The BenQ’s 65W power delivery is well below its 90W competition, and won’t keep a 16-inch MacBook Pro charged under heavy load. You’re also giving up 4K resolution and Thunderbolt, features you’ll others like the Apple Studio Display.
 For basic office use, though, the savings are real. If you’re after a clean, simple MacBook Pro setup on a tight budget, the GW2486TC covers the basics better than anything else we’ve tested at this price.

 Reasons to avoid

 - Mediocre stand, nothing special
 Ok, so the Dell UltraSharp U3226Q 32 4K QD-OLED monitor is far from a cheap 4K display, but it's an absolutely great monitor for creative professionals; whether you are editing photos or videos or getting deep into graphic design.
 A quantum dot 4K OLED display with "spectacular" picture quality per reviewer Collin Probst's testing, is the obvious star of the show. It's a superb panel for photo and video editing, and lends itself well for website design. A detachable shader also help reinforce this monitor's professional chops, but its gets plenty bright without needing the shade, according to Probst.
 Dell has a stellar reputation for making great displays for professionals, so this 32-inch OLED display's quality isn't a huge surprise. What is nice is that the monitor can do a lot via a single Thunderbolt port with power delivery, handy to plug into the somewhat restrained port selection of MacBook Pro laptops. But it also has a host of other ports, from HDMI 2.1 ports to USB-C and more, meaning you can build a comprehensive creator-centric desktop set up around it.
 Over to Probst to have the final word: "If you know you're looking for an absurdly nice monitor because you are a video editor, a photo editor, or a content creator in some way, and you need a high-quality one, then absolutely make sure you check this one out."

 Best monitor for MacBook Pro: FAQs 
 (Image credit: Acer // Future) What is the best resolution for monitors with a MacBook Pro?
 The MacBook Pro is Apple's machine for creators, and that means having excellent visuals for photo and video editing, 3D creative work, and more. To make the most out of what you work on, 4K (3840 x 2160) resolution is the way to go. That said, if you're using your MacBook Pro for anything else, like spreadsheets, writing documents or even coding, you'll be just fine with even a 1080p display. If you're after the highest pixel density, though, 5K and upwards is what you're after. 
 What Power Delivery should the monitor have to charge my MacBook Pro?
 You'll see many monitors with Thunderbolt/USB-C Power Delivery (PD). This means you can plug your MacBook Pro into the monitor and it will charge the laptop while in use. 
 However, the right choice depends on your MacBook Pro's model and CPU. Check out the table below to see which one is right for your laptop. 
Swipe to scroll horizontally
 MacBook Pro model
 Recommended minimum power delivery
 MacBook Pro 13-inch (M1, M2)
 70W
 MacBook Pro 14-inch (M3, M4, M5)
 70W
 MacBook Pro 14-inch (M1, M2, M3, M4, M5 Pro and Max)
 100W
 MacBook Pro 16-inch (M1, M2, M3, M4, M5 Pro and Max)
 140W
 Are there any specific connectivity options that I should look for in a monitor for my MacBook Pro?
 The best monitors for a MacBook Pro will feature USB-C and/or Thunderbolt connectivity. These allow slick, single-cable connectivity that covers charging the MacBook, driving the display, and connecting peripherals. 
 Outside of that, you can find a monitor with a built-in USB-C hub that opens up several ports through the single USB-C used to send video to your monitor. Depending on the monitor, sometimes this can also be used to charge your MacBook Pro.
 Are there any monitors that are specifically designed for use with the MacBook Pro?
 Some monitors, such as the Apple Studio Display and Apple Pro Display XDR, are explicitly designed for use with Apple devices and mirror the wide color P3 gamut and Liquid Retina Display. 
 However, many high-quality monitors from other brands are also compatible with the MacBook Pro. Some monitors will work better with the MacBook Pro than others, but generally, any even semi-recent monitor will be compatible in one way or another with a MacBook Pro.
 How to choose the best monitor for MacBook Pro 
 When choosing which monitor is best for your MacBook Pro, there are a few specs and details you'll want to check.
 Not everyone will need the same specifications. For example, if you're mostly working with office apps, you may not need the broader color space coverage that's required for image or video editing. However you use your monitor, here's what we recommend looking out for.
 Resolution : macOS loves high-resolution displays. The more pixels, the better for rendering nice, clean fonts and providing plenty of image detail. Apple's own desktop displays, the Apple Pro Display XDR and Studio Display, have what's known as Retina pixel density. In practice, that means over 200 pixels per inch (PPI), which matches the screens in the MacBook Pro. Very few non-Apple displays can match that pixel density, but a 27-inch 4K display with 163 pixels per inch is a good baseline.
 Connectivity : USB-C or Thunderbolt with Power Delivery is the bare minimum when it comes to connectivity. We'd recommend at least 65W of power delivery and ideally 90W-plus for keeping your MacBook Pro fully powered. A USB hub with plenty of USB-A and USB-C ports is very desirable, too. Additional inputs like HDMI can be handy, and an Ethernet port can be useful for some office environments. The ability to daisy chain a second monitor is also an interesting option, as is a KVM switch if you're sharing the display with a second computer.
 HDR versus SDR support: HDR is a tricky technology. Many workflows don't require it. But it is becoming more widespread. A display with HDR capability tends to also offer increased colour coverage and generally improve image quality. However, the technologies that enable HDR rendering vary hugely, and some displays are much more effective than others. For that reason, unless you know your workflows require full HDR support, we recommend focusing on getting a display with good SDR performance. If it happens to also offer some HDR capability, great. But for most users, HDR probably isn't a top priority.
 Build quality and extras: It's easy to obsess over specifications like resolution and HDR performance. But the overall quality of a display and feature set can make a big difference, too. If you're paying big bucks, it's nice to have a display that feels worth the money and looks good with your laptop. Likewise, superficially lesser features like good speakers, a great webcam and a microphone array can make a big difference to the overall usability of a monitor. Having features like that built in can also help to reduce desk clutter and simplify docking and connectivity. For more extras, we've reviewed the best MacBook Pro accessories .
 How we test the best monitors for MacBook Pro 
 (Image credit: Future) Our expert team of reviewers has tested a massive range of displays, including the best monitors for photo editing and the best monitors for video editing . So, we're experienced at knowing what to look out for to help you find the best dual monitor set-up to go with your laptop.
 A decent monitor for your MacBook Pro isn't going to be cheap. So, you want to know you're making the right choice. That's why we test each display extensively. That starts with performance assessments of various aspects of image quality.
 That includes brightness, refresh rate, and pixel response. We also consider colour accuracy, viewing angles, contrast, HDR performance, latency, and last but by no means least, resolution and pixel density. Display tech is increasingly varied and complex, what with new technologies like HDR, mini-LED backlights, and OLED panels revolutionising the industry. So, we keep on top of all of that for you, helping you to understand the difference between a few edge-lit dimming zones and a real full-array deal
 Crucially, we also assess how well a display works with macOS. Once connected to a MacBook Pro, does it offer a full range of optimised scaling options, for instance? Next up is connectivity. We consider the range of ports on offer and whether single-cable docking with power delivery is included, along with USB hubs and other features like Ethernet, a KVM switch, and display daisy chaining.
 We also consider any extra features like webcams and speakers. In theory, they can add significant value. But if they're not done well, you're probably just paying for things you'll hardly ever use. You might even end up paying twice if you find you need to buy a dedicated webcam or speakers.
 Next up, there's build quality, design, and ergonomics. A monitor that looks great on the desk with your MacBook Pro is important. But good build quality matters, too. When you are investing a lot of money, you want a display to not just look good, but feel good and last the test of time.
 Then there's ergonomics. At a minimum, a robust and stable stand with a good range of adjustability, including height and tilt, is important. The ability to rotate into portrait mode can be handy, too.
 Of course, how all of those factors fit into the overall value proposition is the final measure. The MacBook Pro is a demanding machine. So, you're not going to get the best out of it with a budget display. But you can also spend a lot of money and not necessarily get a better display solution. We'll help you work out what's worth the money and what costs plenty but doesn't improve your macOS experience.

 You see, it packs the M5 Pro and the M5 Max — two chips we've already benchmarked extensively in the mini-LED MacBook Pros. This is good news for buyers: You don't have to go in without knowing what you're getting.
 Of course, there are some differences that may change results here. For example, this is a significantly lighter laptop with an OLED display — two variables (battery capacity and screen) that may change a couple things here. But we already get a good insight from these numbers.

While there might be some subtle differences in performance that are unrelated to the two processors, we expect raw numbers to be similar to what we've already seen in our MacBook Pro M5 benchmarks .
 Want more Apple news?
 Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.
 Apple did say that the new MacBook Pros have a completely redesigned thermal system, so that could let the M5 Pro and the M5 Max stretch their legs and still maintain that same performance even in a significantly lighter chassis.
 To see how they stack up, we pulled our Geekbench 6 results. These benchmarks measure single-core and multi-core performance. There's also our Handbrake test, which times how long a laptop takes to transcode a 4K video to 1080p.
 Let's have a look at the base M5 (which you won't find in the new OLED MacBook Pros, but it's a good starting point to compare to), the M5 Pro, the M5 Max, and even the M4 Pro and the M6 to give a well-rounded overview.

 The first thing that jumps out: Single-core scores are nearly identical across the entire M5 family, so this is what we can expect from the new OLED MacBook Pros, too. It's unlikely to feel snappier in such tasks than a base M5 model.
 The real gap lies in multi-core, and it's huge . Just look at the numbers: The M5 Pro and M5 Max both land close to 30,000, which is about 25% ahead of the M4 Pro, roughly in line with the up to 30% Apple promised when it launched these chips back in March.
 As a reminder, both the M5 Pro and the M5 Max feature the same 18-core CPU. The extra money buys you extra GPU cores and more memory.
 The M6 in the Mac mini and the new 14-inch MacBook Pro tops the single-core benchmarks, but it trails both the M5 Pro/Max chips by a wide margin in multi-core.
 To summarize: The MacBook Pros released in March were absolute powerhouses. We expect the same of the OLED models.
 Apple M5 Pro and M5 Max: Graphics and AI 
 (Image credit: Future) CPU comparisons are pretty tight between the two chips, but in graphics, we'll find a definite leader. The M5 Max sports up to twice as many GPU cores, and yes, that does lead to huge performance gains.

 Both chips beat every Windows laptop in our first table on graphics, which bodes well for the new OLED MacBook Pros. However, Nvidia's new RTX Spark is a different story.
 In our more recent testing, it outscored the M5 Pro in both 3DMark Steel Nomad and Solar Bay Extreme. Given the scores and the massively ramped-up GPU performance on the M5 Max, chances are that Apple would win in such a match-up, too.
 AI is more nuanced. The M5 Pro scored almost exactly the same as the base M5 in Geekbench AI, and Qualcomm's Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme leads the pack.
 Apple M5 Pro and M5 Max: Battery life 
 (Image credit: Future) MacBooks are known for their outstanding battery life, so it won't surprise you to hear that in our testing, the LCD models from earlier this year did a great job.
 Our 16-inch M5 Pro lasted 21 hours and 25 minutes in our web-surfing test at 150 nits of brightness. That's more than double what Nvidia's RTX Spark and Qualcomm's Snapdragon X2 Elite managed.
 The powerful, yet more demanding M5 Max lasted just under 18 hours.
 While we can predict the performance of the OLED MacBook Pros with a certain degree of accuracy, the battery life is harder to call. Apple rates the new models at up to 24 hours, which is the same as the mini-LED 16-inch MacBook Pro, and that's despite the lighter chassis. OLED panels use less power on dark content but more on bright, white screens, so we'll need to test it ourselves to see how that 24-hour claim holds up in real life.
 Apple OLED MacBook Pro: Outlook 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) With performance numbers such as these, we fully expect the new PROLED XDR MacBook Pros to be next-level in the best way possible.
 As they're equipped with chips we're already familiar with, raw performance numbers should stay roughly the same as before.
 With that said, the new OLED models are also pricier . The maxed-out 16-inch model actually goes up to $14,549, but all the new models cost $400 more across the board for the screen upgrade alone.
 But you're not paying for more firepower—you're paying for the tandem OLED panel and a couple more goodies, such as a touchscreen and the lack of a display notch. If you're only interested in how capable your laptop is, stick to the LCD versions, as you're getting the exact same chips.

 After weeks of speculation, Apple has confirmed its new MacBook Pro OLED . The touchscreen laptop boasts a PROLED XDR display panel that provides up to 2,000 nits peak HDR and SDR brightness.
 MacBook Pro OLED preorders are live right now with an official release date of November 6. You can choose between a 14-inch MacBook Pro OLED from $2,899 or a 16-inch MacBook Pro OLED from $3,339. The laptops can be customized with Apple's M5 Pro or M5 Max CPU. The base models for both laptops include 24GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD.
 Currently, MacBook Pro OLED preorders can be made via Amazon, Best Buy, and the Apple Store. In some cases, you can even score a free gift card with your preorder.
 Quick Links

 Best Buy: from $2,899 + $100 gift card

 MacBook Pro OLED Preorders 
 Apple 14" MacBook Pro OLED: $2,899 at Amazon The MacBook Pro OLED is one of the biggest MacBook releases in recent years. It can be configured with an M5 Pro (from $2,899) or M5 Max (from $4,499) CPU and packs a 14.2-inch PROLED XDR touchscreen display with 3024 x 1986 resolution, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB SSD. You also get three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports, HDMI port, and an SDXC slot. The laptop will be available on November 6.

You also get three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports, HDMI port, and an SDXC slot. The laptop will be available on November 6.

Otherwise, it may be awhile before Amazon offers a notable discount.

(You can also trade-in other Apple devices such as iPhones and iPads). For example, my 15-inch MacBook Air (M2) in good condition is worth $600.  Apple has unveiled an October refresh of its 14-inch MacBook Pro complete with the M6 processor that brings the laptop in line with the Mac mini and today's also-announced M6 iMac.
 As part of Apple's "Pro and tell" announcements this week , we now have a brand new MacBook Pro to compliment the iMac and yesterday's iPad mini 8 reveal . If the rumors are true, then we may be in line for one more MacBook-related reveal this week: the highly-anticipated touchscreen MacBook Pro OLED.
 But let's return to this device which, sadly, doesn't come with a touchscreen or much in the way of a new design. Reportedly, Apple is saving its MacBook Pro redesign for the M7 version of the machine next year . But then again, criticizing the MacBook Pro for its design seems churlish — the thin and light aluminum unibody enclosure conceals a vast amount of power and is just as good to look at now as it's always been.
 Latest Videos From Tom's Guide 
 Watch full video here: 
 As with the new iMac, the M6 MacBook Pro will ship with macOS 27 Golden Gate, which includes the next version of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI .
 Here's everything we know about the new M6 MacBook Pro.
 You may like
 MacBook Pro M6 vs MacBook Pro M5: Biggest upgrades you need to know 
 How to pre-order M6 MacBook Pro — secure Apple's latest laptop well in time for release day 
 Apple unveils new iMac with M6 — here are all the upgrades 
 M6 MacBook Pro: Price and release date 
 (Image credit: Apple) The new M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999 or $38.99 per month for 12 months. That gets you the default configuration of an M6 chip, 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage.
 In the U.K., the pricing starts at £1,999 and pre-orders in both regions begin on Wednesday, October 28. Shipping will begin on November 6.
 Want more Apple news?
 Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.
 In line with just about every other consumer electronics release this year, that's a price increase over the $1,599 starting cost of last year's 14-inch M5 MacBook Pro. Of course, since then Apple put the pricing up by $300 in June which makes this technically not a price hike... but still — it's a higher cost in my book thanks to ongoing component and memory shortages driven by AI demand.
 M6 MacBook Pro: Performance 
 (Image credit: Apple) The biggest single reason for picking up the M6 MacBook Pro is in the name: Apple's M6 chip follows the A20 Pro inside the iPhone Duo and moves to a 2-nanometer architecture that'll deliver a notable power and efficiency gain over previous models.
 We've seen the M6 chip only in one Mac product so far; the latest Mac mini and in our review we noted its performance "really shone" and "didn't miss a beat" even when we put it under extreme multitasking.
 What to read next

 Is it finally time to upgrade from M1? Apple's MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR sure is tempting 
 Here's a breakdown of how the chip inside the Mac mini held up against the same benchmarking tests as the M5 and M5 Pro chips inside last year's MacBook Pro.

 Specific performance will, of course, be slightly different for this machine but the above results should give you an indication of how much more powerful it's likely to be over last year's MacBook Pro. It likely won't be enough to convince M5 owners to jump, but anyone still using an M1 or M2 MacBook Pro will find the M6 is the upgrade they've been waiting for.
 The M5 chip consisted of a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU while the M6 improves that by two additional cores in both the CPU and the GPU. In addition, it's got a Dual 16-core Neural Engine for AI and machine learning that could take the fight to Nvidia's RTX Spark machines that are specifically targeting on-device AI workloads.
 Apple says the 12-core GPU delivers up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to 25 percent faster AI workloads when compared to M5.
 The Neural Engine is also supported by Neural Accelerators in each GPU core that should mean the M6 MacBook Pro is streets ahead when it comes to using AI-powered creative tools.
 M6 MacBook Pro: Design 
 (Image credit: Apple) We could have seen this one coming a mile away, but Apple hasn't changed up the outward design of the MacBook Pro for the 2026 iteration. In fact, it's largely the same as the design we've had since 2021: a solid slab of machined aluminium that's both sturdy and light given the amount of power under the hood.
 The M6 MacBook Pro retains the same 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61 inch dimensions and 3.4 pound weight as the previous generation and the color options remain a choice between Silver and Space Black.
 Apple has kept the 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display running at 120Hz ProMotion for the M6 MacBook Pro refresh. We still have the notch cutout at the top, squashing the rumor Apple would switch it up for an iPhone-style Dynamic Island this time around. And, as mentioned up top, there's no touchscreen here for interacting with macOS 27 Golden Gate.
 When it comes to ports, the M6 MacBook Pro keeps the current physical I/O layout: you get three Thunderbolt 4/USB4 ports, an HDMI port, an SDXC card slot, a 3.5mm headphone jack, and MagSafe 3 charging.
 M6 MacBook Pro: Networking and battery life 
 (Image credit: Apple) Alongside the performance from the new M6 chip, the MacBook Pro also benefits from receiving Apple's N1 chip and a boost to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 .
 The current model still uses Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3 so the M6 refresh will give users lower networking latency and higher throughput. Bluetooth 6 leads to better distance tracking and more power efficiency for wireless accessories like game controllers or a pair of headphones.
 Apple says the M6 MacBook Pro's battery life gets up to 14 additional hours for Intel-based upgraders and up to four more hours for users coming from M1, delivering up to 24 hours overall, so users can get more done on a single charge.
 M6 MacBook Pro: Outlook 
 The MacBook Pro refresh is pretty customary once October rolls around and Apple has delivered more or less what we expected here: no big design changes but whole host of extra power and battery life efficiency.
 We'll reserve judgement until we've got the new M6 MacBook Pro into the Tom's Guide lab for benchmarking but it's safe to say the new chip is going to deliver in some pretty clear-cut ways.
 Anyone upgrading from an M1, M2 or older Intel MacBook Pro will see a dramatic leap in performance and read/write speeds. Creative professionals and anyone working with local AI will benefit from the additional power of Apple's new chip.
 However, for those already using an M4 or M5 machine, there may be less of a reason to upgrade. Especially since the potential reveal of a MacBook Pro OLED tomorrow could easily eclipse today's news for many MacBook fans.

 Apple is updating two more computers to its M6 system-on-chip. The base 14-inch MacBook Pro and the iMac lineup are getting the company's latest processor ahead of tomorrow's "Pro and Tell" event in Los Angeles.
These devices are retaining the same designs that they've had for years. The computers will be available for pre-order on Wednesday at 10:10 a.m. PT (1:10 p.m. ET) and will ship on Nov. 6. The M6 in the MacBook Pro will be configured with 12 CPU cores and 12 GPU cores, alongside dual neural engines for certain on-device AI workloads. On the iMac, there will also be a cut-down option with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU.
 (Image credit: Apple) The MacBook Pro will be configurable with up to 32GB of RAM and is being updated with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 using Apple's N1 networking chip. The iMac is also getting those networking benefits, as well as a 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet port. Like previous iMacs, the number of ports you get is tied to the chip, with two Thunderbolt 4 ports with the base chip or four with the option with more cores.
It's no surprise that Apple is pushing both of these as AI-forward machines, both with the new chips and the recently released Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features in macOS 27 Golden Gate.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 will start at $1,999 ($1,899 with education discount), while the iMac will begin at $1,499 ($1,449 with education discount) for the 10-core CPU/GPU configuration and $1,699 ($1,599 with education discount) for the full chip.
 Both of these new systems are being announced the day before Apple is expected to release a MacBook with an OLED touchscreen. Yesterday, in a week of announcements, Apple debuted a redesign of the iPad Mini with a thinner body and an OLED display.

High-end professionals should always aim for Thunderbolt 5.
 The dock needs one (“ upstream “) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although all recent MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe 3 port), and at least another (“ downstream “) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).
 The USB-C MacBook Neo has just the one data port, with the other reserved for charging. A dock with Power Delivery will greatly expand the entry-level Mac laptop.
 For more detail, read our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 vs USB4 explainer .
 Add external displays to your MacBook
 If you use your laptop as your principal computer, attaching at least one larger display to create a hybrid desktop/laptop setup, with a keyboard and mouse, will boost your productivity. You can turn that 13in MacBook’s cramped screen real-estate into an iconic iMac-sized 27in or even larger screen by adding an extra display—or connect two or even four large monitors to extend your screen across your whole desk. Take a look at our recommended best monitors and displays for Mac and also the best portable monitors for Mac .
 You’ll get two or more Extended mode screens (where the screen extends beyond what you can see on the laptop screen) using a Thunderbolt connection (or DisplayPort/HDMI). Natively over mere USB-C, Macs can connect to only one external display in Extended mode, as opposed to Mirrored mode (which replicates exactly what you get on the laptop screen) but DisplayLink is third-party software that allows some docks to extend to up to four screens on even the most basic Mac. DisplayLink-supporting docks are also the only way that non-Pro/Max M1 and M2 MacBooks can connect more than one external display.
 More explained: we cover more on Mac docking stations and external displays at the end of this feature below our recommendations.
 Do I need a docking station?
 With three TB4 or TB5 and an HDMI port, a MacBook with a Max chip could connect to up to four external displays without the need for a dock, although such a power user would likely require extra Thunderbolt and other ports for more devices to make up for using all the laptop ports for multiple monitors. See below our list of recommended docking stations for more detail on the external display options with each recent MacBook .
 All docks come with a bunch of USB ports: some old-school USB-A and newer, more capable USB-C . MacBook Pros also have an SD card reader . Although this card reader is rated as UHS-II (312MBps), Apple has pegged it back at 250MBps, so for the fastest speeds (and a microSD slot if you need one), a dock will likely be a better choice for memory-card use if it is rated at UHS-II rather than UHS-I (104MBps).
 MacBooks also lack wired Internet access via an Ethernet port, so if you want to escape flaky Wi-Fi, buy a dock with at least Gigabit Ethernet, although you could add a Thunderbolt-to-Ethernet adapter instead if you have a spare TB port. Some later docks include faster 2.5Gb, 5Gb or even 10Gb Ethernet but you’ll need a supporting router or other device to get the benefits, although these faster Ethernet ports are backwards compatible with Gigabit so will future-proof your purchase.
 While docking stations are most often attached to MacBooks, they can be useful with a desktop Mac. The Mac mini especially can benefit from the extra ports and built-in SSD slot options. We cover these specifically in our feature on how to upgrade the Mac mini , including reviews of the best hubs and docks that fit the mini. 
 Dock or hub?
 If you need just a few extra ports, a USB-C hub or Thunderbolt hub might be your best choice—see our roundup of the best USB-C and Thunderbolt hubs for Mac . However, if you require a bunch of fast ports including Gigabit (or faster) Ethernet and multiple video ports plus more powerful charging capability, then look for a full dock that fulfils your needs. We’ve reviewed the best hubs alongside the docks.

 USB PD: Power Delivery for your laptop
 Most docks can charge the connected MacBook, so look for the right Power Delivery (PD) rating that suits your laptop. You can’t over-power a MacBook so the simplest advice is to aim as high as you can. 70W will be more than enough to fast-charge a MacBook Air but go for 85W or more (PD 3.0) for a MacBook Pro, and 140W (PD 3.1) for the top-end 16-inch Pro.

The downside is that you must use two of your Mac’s Thunderbolt ports to use the FusionDock Ultra. If only one cable is connected, some ports on the dock will not function.

 A KVM docking station enables you to instantly share a single set of peripherals—the KVM stands for Keyboard, Video (monitors) and Mouse—between two computers. While most docks allow you to connect different computers, a KVM dock makes it easier with a special “Switch”—a button that you push to instantly take control from the other computer. The KVM Switch virtually disconnects the first computer and connects the second without you having to unplug any cables.
 The iDock M10 from AV Access is a Mac-dedicated KVM dock that you can connect to a MacBook and a desktop computer, including a Windows PC. It comes with a KVM Wired Remote Controller, which is the button you press to toggle between computers. The dock features 15 ports but four of them are used as upstream connections to the two computers. 
 Setup requires two MacBook Thunderbolt ports and dedicated connections to both computers. Major limitations include weak device charging, limited port flexibility, no support for two laptops,

 Which ports are on each MacBook?
 Of Apple’s recent laptop ranges, the M1/M2/M3 MacBook Air and 14-inch M3 MacBook Pro feature two ports that Apple specified as “ Thunderbolt / USB 4 ” ports, while more recent the 13in and 15in M4/M5 MacBook Air models feature two Thunderbolt 4 ports . The 14in and 16in M1/M2/M3 Pro, plain M4/M5 MacBook Pro, and M1/M2/M3 Max MacBook Pro models come with three Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) ports. Ignore Apple’s dual designation of non-4 Thunderbolt and USB4—it just means that the ports don’t certify as pure Thunderbolt 4, and that shouldn’t worry most users except for the number of external displays each supports.
 Apple’s latest M4/M5 Pro and M4/M5 Max MacBook Pro models feature three of the latest Thunderbolt 5 ports, which are backwards compatible with TB4, TB3 and USB-C. They promise 80Gbps data transfer and 120Gbps video rates. Until the technology finds its way into more devices and the Thunderbolt 5 dock market matures, you are still going to do very well with a 40Gbps Thunderbolt 4 dock, but Thunderbolt 5 docks are fast becoming the norm for new releases.
 Thunderbolt 5 frees the latest top-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBooks from the two-display limitation forced on them by the macOS’s lack of MST (Multi Stream Transport) support. The M5 Pro now supports up to three external displays over a single Thunderbolt connection and the M5 Max up to four. To reach four external displays most docks reviewed here would need to daisy-chain the fourth display off one of the others.
 The entry-level MacBook Neo utilizes lower-spec USB-C rather than Thunderbolt, with 10Gbps rather than Thunderbolt’s 40Gbps or 80Gbps. A USB-C dock is therefore all you should need but it will work with Thunderbolt, which is backwards compatible, but limited to the Neo’s 10Gbps bandwidth.
 The latest MacBook Pro models boast three Thunderbolt 5 ports. Apple

 MacBook Neo: Two USB-C ports, plus headphone jack. One USB-C port is charging only; the other supports video and data up to 10Gbps as well as charging.
 13-inch and 15-inch M1/M2/M3 MacBook Air: Two Thunderbolt/USB4 ports and one MagSafe 3 charging port, plus headphone jack
 13-inch and 15-inch M4/M5 MacBook Air: Two Thunderbolt 4 ports and one MagSafe 3 charging port, plus headphone jack
 13-inch M1/M2 MacBook Pro: Two Thunderbolt/USB4 ports and one MagSafe 3 charging port, plus headphone jack

 14-inch M1/M2/M3 Pro, M1/M2/M3 Max and plain M4/M5/M6 MacBook Pro: Three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, one HDMI port, one SDXC card slot, plus headphone jack
 14-inch M4/M5 Pro or M4/M5 Max MacBook Pro: Three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports, one HDMI port, one SDXC card slot, plus headphone jack

 How many external displays can each MacBook support without a dock?
 Neo: One external display with up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. Use a DisplayLink dock for more than one monitor on the MacBook Neo.
 M1/M2: One external display with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz. Use a DisplayLink dock for more than one monitor on these MacBooks.
 M3: Supports up to two external displays, one with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz and one at 5K/60Hz when the MacBook lid is closed .
 M4: Supports up to two external displays, one with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz and one at 5K/60Hz.
 M5: Supports up to two external 6K/60Hz or 4K/144Hz displays, or one 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz, 4K/240Hz.
 M6: Supports up to two external 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz displays, or one 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz, 4K/240Hz.
 M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro: Up to two external displays with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt, or one external display with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt and one external display with up to 4K resolution at 144Hz over HDMI. Or one external display supported at 8K resolution at 60Hz or one external display at 4K resolution at 240Hz over HDMI.
 M1/M2/M3/M4 Max: Up to four external displays: Up to three external displays with 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt and one external display with up to 4K resolution at 144Hz over HDMI. Up to three external displays: Up to two external displays with 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt and one external display with up to 8K resolution at 60Hz or one external display with 4K resolution at 240Hz over HDMI.
 M5 Pro: Supports up to three external displays over a single Thunderbolt port. Up to three displays up to a native resolution of 6K (6144 x 3456) at 60Hz or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 144Hz over Thunderbolt or HDMI. Or one external display supported at 8K (7680 x 4320) at 60Hz, 5K (5120 x 2880) at 120Hz, or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 240Hz, plus a second display up to a native resolution of 5K (5120 x 2880) at 120Hz or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 200Hz over Thunderbolt or HDMI.
 M5 Max: Supports up to four external displays over a single Thunderbolt port. Up to four displays up to a native resolution of 6K (6144 x 3456) at 60Hz or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 144Hz over Thunderbolt or HDMI. Two displays up to a native resolution of 8K (7680 x 4320) at 60Hz, 5K (5120 x 2880) at 120Hz, or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 240Hz over Thunderbolt or HDMI.
 Mac docking stations and external displays
 Baseus
 While Apple’s MacBooks featuring the company’s own M-series Silicon chips are super speedy compared to the models sporting Intel processors, models with plain (non-Pro or -Max) M1 and M2 chips come with an incredible limitation: they don’t support more than one external display in Extended Mode even via their Thunderbolt ports. Plain M3 MacBooks can support two displays but only with their lids closed. The MacBook Neo uses a different A18 Pro chip and has the same single-monitor limitation as the plain M1 and M2.
 This limitation means that when using any docking station, M1/M2 and Neo MacBook users cannot extend their desktop over two or more displays, and will be limited to either dual Mirrored displays or one external display—although adding third-party DisplayLink or InstantView software to the Mac and connecting to a dedicated USB-C dock will allow you to add more than one external monitor to an M1, M2 or M3 MacBook . Follow that link for our roundup of the best USB-C DisplayLink docks , and we’ve included our favorite in our roundup above.
 In the example above, standard M1/M2/Neo Macs would require DisplayLink to achieve Extended Mode 2. M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro/Max and standard M3/M4/M5 onwards can natively work in that mode without DisplayLink but would require it for three or more extended screens. M5 Pro supports three screens, and M5 Max supports four, without requiring DisplayLink.
 Above, we’ve listed the native external display options for each MacBook. Thunderbolt 5 docks should support up to four 6K displays if you own an M5 Max-chip MacBook Pro.
 While some docking stations promise support for 8K displays, Macs are limited to 6K support via the dock. Macs with an M2/M3/M4 Pro or Max chip can support an 8K display at 60Hz but only when it is connected via the Mac’s own HDMI port and not any port on the dock.
 Dock, hub or dongle: Whole lotta ports
 You need one (“ upstream “) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although the 14/16in MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe port), and likely at least another (“ downstream “) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).
 There are many inexpensive USB-C dongles/hubs that let you add more devices to a MacBook (see our roundup of the best USB-C adapters for Macs ) or a Thunderbolt hub offering a few extra ports might be all your need, but for maximum flexibility check out a docking station that takes care of all your extra port requirements, and allows you to simply attach it to your laptop with just one cable when you get to the office or come home.
 Docks aren’t just for MacBooks. Mac mini (2018 and later) and iMac (2017 and later) owners may also consider expanding their ports with a Thunderbolt docking station.
 The inclusion of an SD or microSD card reader isn’t just for camera buffs. It’s a convenient and affordable way to add storage to your laptop setup. We found a 512GB Samsung Evo microSD card on Amazon for around $100 in the US and under £100  in the UK. That’s a very cheap way of adding half a terabyte of portable storage. For more details read up on our best microSD cards .
 Some of the docks reviewed above include an integrated SSD enclosure that lets you add up to 8TB of fast storage to your connected MacBook.
 Charging the laptop
 While the MacBook Neo can get by on 20W Power Delivery (PD), the M1/M2/M3/M4/M5 MacBook Air requires a PD charger with at least 30W power, but you can fast-charge an M2 and later Air with a charger rated at over 70W. You’ll need 67W for the 13-inch MacBook Pro and 70W for the 14-inch MBP (with 8-, 10-, 11-or 12-core CPU), 96W for 14-inch MBP (with 12- or 14-core CPU), and 96W (preferably 140W) for the 16-inch MBP. The older 15in MacBook Pro requires a 87W PD charger.
 If you own a larger MacBook Pro, buy a dock with a PD (Power Delivery) potential of at least 85W if you can. USB PD 3.0 maxes at 100W, while USB PD 3.1 can support up to 240W of power. The 16-inch MacBook Pro requires 140W to fast-charge, so owners of that laptop should look for a PD 3.1 charger.
 If you just need a spare charger, we’ve tested the best MacBook chargers for you.
 Other dock options
 Here we concentrate on Thunderbolt docks, but also include cheaper USB-C docks—which Thunderbolt MacBooks can use, but at the cost of reduced bandwidth and display limitations. We’ve also included our favorite Thunderbolt hubs for smaller and cheaper alternatives. For more non-Thunderbolt USB-C-only docks check out Tech Advisor’s roundup of the best USB-C docking stations for laptops . Tech Advisor also reviews all the available Thunderbolt 4 docks .
 Now think about a stand to go alongside the dock
 These MacBook docking stations look and work great with a laptop stand, and we’ve also tested some MacBook-friendly stands that lack all the extra ports but keep your MacBook/Air/Pro upright and out of the way: further saving valuable desk space, reducing clutter, keeping your laptop cool, and saving it from spills.

Best TB5 Dock for MacBook Pro 2026: CalDigit TS5 Skip to main content 
 For a MacBook Pro, buy the CalDigit TS5 . It is $399.95, it charges at 140W, and CalDigit’s own listing names the 16-inch M3, M4, and M5 Pro and Max as the laptops that want that wattage. Fanless, three downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports, a DisplayPort 2.1, and a 2.5GbE jack so the Mac finally has Ethernet. The Anker Prime TB5 is the same money on its main listing and a worse fit the day you plug anything in that is not a Mac.
 Affiliate disclosure
 Some links below are Amazon affiliate links, including /go/ redirects that land on Amazon. Buying through them pays me a small commission at no extra cost to you. Prices were checked on September 21, 2026 and move constantly, so confirm them on the product page.
 The wider field, including cheaper certified docks, is in the Thunderbolt 5 docks guide . The head-to-head that ignores the Mac-only question is CalDigit TS5 vs Anker Prime . This page is the MacBook Pro decision.

 The wattage that matters is 140W, and only on the 16-inch
 Apple’s fast-charge page lists a 140W USB-C adapter and a 96W USB-C adapter for the 14-inch MacBook Pro (2021 and later) ( Apple ). A 16-inch is the machine that actually draws 140W. ChargerLab’s March 2025 test of a 16-inch M4 Pro measured 140W on both the MagSafe port and the USB-C ports, with a PD 3.1 supply ( ChargerLab ). CalDigit repeats the point on the TS5 and the TS5 Plus: 140W host charging, called out for the 16-inch M3, M4, and M5 Pro and Max.
 A 14-inch will charge from any of these docks and will fast-charge from less than 140W. A 16-inch on a 96W dock charges, and under a heavy compile it can still drain. Thunderbolt 5’s spec goes to 240W. The Mac does not take 240W. Paying for a dock that advertises 240W host power does not charge a MacBook Pro any faster than a 140W dock.
 Use the cable that came in the box. A random USB-C cable from a phone will often charge and then fall back to USB 2 or a lower power contract. The TS5 ships with a 1m braided cable and a 240W power supply. The TS5 Plus ships with a 330W supply so the 140W host budget does not collapse when the downstream ports are busy.
 MagSafe can stay in the laptop bag. One Thunderbolt cable is the point of the dock. If you charge by MagSafe and use the dock only for data, you have bought a very expensive USB hub.
 Which MacBook Pro you actually have
 A Thunderbolt 5 dock works on an older MacBook Pro. It does not turn that laptop into a Thunderbolt 5 laptop. The link falls back to whatever the ports on the machine are.
 MacBook Pro 
 Ports 
 What a TB5 dock gets you 
 14-inch with the plain M4 
 Three Thunderbolt 4 ports, 40Gb/s 
 Charging, displays, Ethernet. Storage tops out at Thunderbolt 4. You paid for headroom. 
 M4 Pro or M4 Max, 14-inch or 16-inch 
 Three Thunderbolt 5 ports, up to 120Gb/s with bandwidth boost 
 The full dock. This is the machine the TS5 is for. 
 2021 through 2023, M1 Pro/Max, M2 Pro/Max, M3 Pro/Max 
 Thunderbolt 4 
 Same story as the plain M4. Buy the dock if you are about to replace the laptop. Otherwise a Thunderbolt 4 dock does the same job for less. 
 M5 Pro or M5 Max 
 CalDigit’s own listing names these as 140W machines 
 Treat them like the M4 Pro/Max until you confirm the port speed in System Information. 
 Apple’s tech specs for the 14-inch M4 Pro are the other half of the charging story. The 12-core M4 Pro ships with a 70W adapter, the 14-core ships with 96W, and Apple says fast charge wants 96W or higher ( 14-inch M4 Pro/Max specs ). The 16-inch is the one that wants 140W. A 140W dock covers both. A 96W dock is enough for the 14-inch and short for a 16-inch under compile.
 Look before you pay. Apple menu, About This Mac, then System Report, Thunderbolt/USB4. If the speed says 40 Gb/s, you do not have Thunderbolt 5, no matter what the dock box prints.
 How many screens the chip allows
 The dock cannot invent displays the SoC does not have. Apple’s support page, updated March 10, 2026, is the list that matters ( How many displays can be connected to MacBook Pro ). Closing the lid does not add a screen on M4 or M5. It does on the base M3, which is a nasty surprise if you bought a dual-monitor dock and leave the laptop open.

 What that means for this page

 A Studio Display and one more monitor. The TS5’s DisplayPort plus one downstream port covers it. Quad-display docks are wasted.

 TS5 is still enough. You do not need 26 ports to light three screens.

 This is the chip an iVANKY quad-6K claim is aimed at.

 Up to four, and Apple’s four-screen row uses the HDMI port for the last one 
 Count the laptop’s own HDMI. A dock that only has Thunderbolt may stop at three. 
 Base M3 
 Two only with the lid closed 
 If the second screen is black with the lid open, the dock is not broken. 
 I would avoid DisplayLink. It is a software display that needs a driver, and none of the docks here need it. Native Thunderbolt or the DisplayPort on the TS5 is the path.
 The MacBook Pro already has HDMI and an SD card slot. A dock earns the $400 when it replaces a pile of dongles: Ethernet, a couple of USB-A devices, a second monitor, and the power brick, on one cable. If the desk is one monitor on the built-in HDMI and MagSafe charging, a USB-C Ethernet adapter is the honest purchase and this page is the wrong one. For the rest of the desk around either setup, the tech gadgets worth owning before 2027 roundup covers the portable monitor, charger and lighting picks that pair with (or replace) a dock.
 What goes on the cable
 The dock’s Ethernet is for the laptop. It is not your homelab core. 2.5GbE is plenty for a MacBook that sometimes copies a project. If Time Machine, a photo library, or a video scratch disk live on a NAS, that is the TS5 Plus or the iVANKY, and the switch those plug into is a different purchase. The 2.5/10GbE switch guide is that purchase. A fast external SSD wants a downstream Thunderbolt port of its own, not a ride through the display chain. The TB5 enclosure guide covers the disk side. Use the cable from the dock box. A Thunderbolt 4 cable will link, and it will cap the pipe at 40Gb/s.
 1. CalDigit TS5
 $399.95 · 4.3 stars from 81 ratings · in stock · 15 ports · fanless · 140W
 CalDigit TS5 
 CalDigit’s port list: one host Thunderbolt 5 port and three downstream ports at 80Gb/s, three 10Gb/s USB-C ports, one 10Gb/s USB-A, one 480Mb/s USB-A, DisplayPort 2.1, SD 4.0 and microSD 4.0 UHS-II readers, 2.5GbE, and three audio jacks. The host port does 140W. The case is aluminum and fanless, which matters on a desk next to a microphone.
 Three downstream TB5 ports is the practical difference from the Anker. One can be a display, one an NVMe enclosure , one a dock or a hub you already own. The card readers are UHS-II. If you offload a camera, that is the difference between a coffee and a long wait.
 It also works on Windows and Linux with a USB4 or Thunderbolt host, at reduced features on older controllers. I care about that even on a Mac page, because the second laptop on a lot of these desks is not a Mac. The TS5 does not punish you for it.
 The failure owners actually post is not “it never worked.” It is the Monday morning after sleep. On r/CalDigit, an M4 Max owner found the TS5 Plus killed keyboard and mouse after deep sleep when the cable was in the right-hand Thunderbolt port, and the left-hand port was fine ( that report ). A TS5 Plus firmware update has also knocked out a dual-monitor setup on a 16-inch M2 Pro until the dock was power-cycled ( another report ). External disks that vanish from Finder after a reboot, until you pull the dock’s power cable, are the same family of bug.
 Before you return a CalDigit, do the boring sequence. Plug into the other side of the Mac. Pull the dock’s own power cable, not just the laptop cable, and wait thirty seconds. Then decide. A dock that only fails on one port is a port or a cable, and a dock that fails on both after every sleep is the one you send back. CalDigit’s utility is worth installing on a Mac. It is also the thing people reinstall when a display stops enumerating, so keep it.
 Best for MacBook Pro

 ★★★★★ ★★★★★

 • A phone cable in the host port will not give you 80Gb/s or 140W.

 2. Anker Prime TB5: buy it for the shape, not a discount
 $399.99 on the main listing · 4.1 stars from 465 ratings · in stock · 14 ports · active cooling
 Anker Prime TB5 dock 
 Anker’s listing: one upstream Thunderbolt 5, two downstream Thunderbolt 5, two USB-C, three USB-A, SD and TF readers, 2.5GbE, audio, and a single HDMI 2.1 or DisplayPort 2.1. One video port, shared. Check which SKU you are holding. Host charging is 140W. There is a fan, and Anker is open about the active cooler.
 A second, thinly reviewed listing was $347.86 the same day. I would not chase it. The listing people have actually bought, 465 of them, is $399.99. At that price the TS5 gives you a third TB5 port, UHS-II readers, no fan, and a host port that is happier about non-Mac machines.
 The comparison documents Anker’s own limit: no Linux, no ChromeOS, no Thunderbolt 3 Windows hosts. On a desk that is only a MacBook Pro, that limit never fires. The fan and the missing third TB5 port still do.
 What owners measured after that is more useful than the port diagram. In r/anker, one person ran iperf3 on the Prime’s 2.5GbE port and got about 140 MB/s, half of what 2.5GbE should do, on a cable and a switch port that hit full speed from a mini PC’s own 2.5GbE NIC ( the thread ). Another unit in the same thread has coil whine as soon as it is powered. A third is happy: 140W held a laptop at full battery through exports that used to drain on an 85W dock, and an Odyssey G9 57-inch ran at full resolution from the DisplayPort, not from the HDMI port. So the Anker can be the right cube, and it can also be a dock whose Ethernet is a 1GbE port wearing a 2.5GbE label. If the Mac’s network copy speed is why you are here, buy the TS5 and test it, or buy the TS5 Plus and skip the argument. If you buy the Anker, run iperf the first evening and return it while the window is open if the number is 140 MB/s.
 Check Anker Prime TB5 price 
 3. TS5 Plus or iVANKY, when the laptop is on the NAS
 Two docks clear 2.5GbE. They solve different desks.
 CalDigit TS5 Plus, $499.99 , 4.2 stars from 277 ratings. Twenty ports: three downstream TB5, five USB-A at 10Gb/s, five USB-C at 10Gb/s, DisplayPort 2.1, UHS-II readers, and 10GbE. The supply is 330W. CalDigit’s title says Mac and PC. This is the one I would buy if the MacBook Pro is the machine that edits off a 10GbE NAS and a PC sometimes sits in the same spot. One hundred dollars over the TS5, and the Ethernet port is the reason.
 CalDigit TS5 Plus 
 iVANKY FusionDock Ultra, $649.99 (list $749.99), 4.3 stars from 279 ratings. Twenty-six ports, dual-chip, 10GbE, and iVANKY’s compatibility note is blunt: this dock is for Macs. Their display claim for an M-series Max MacBook Pro is quad 6K at 60Hz or dual 8K at 60Hz, which lines up with what Apple allows on an M4 Max or M5 Max and does not line up with an M4 Pro’s two-screen cap. The longer writeup is the FusionDock Ultra review . I would buy it when the chip is a Max, the monitor count is the problem, and you have accepted that a Windows laptop will not dock here. I would not buy it to gain 10GbE alone. The TS5 Plus does that for $150 less and keeps the PC option.
 Check TS5 Plus price 
 Check FusionDock Ultra price 
 The Kensington SD5000T5 is the cheap certified TB5 dock in the main docks guide , and it does 140W. The guide’s price is from earlier in 2026. Open the listing and read today’s number before you count on that discount.
 CalDigit TS5 Plus 
 ★★★★★ ★★★★★ 
 4.2 · Very good 
 20-port Thunderbolt 5 dock with 10GbE, 140W charging, and a 330W supply. The MacBook Pro dock when the NAS is the reason you bought 10GbE.
 Check Price on Amazon Price & availability at Amazon.com
 Key Features
 10GbE plus 140W host charging 
 3 downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports 
 5x USB-A and 5x USB-C at 10Gb/s 
 DisplayPort 2.1 and UHS-II SD / microSD 
 330W power supply, works with Mac and PC 
 What we like
 10GbE on a CalDigit, not a Mac-only brand 
 277 ratings, a fuller sample than the TS5 
 The 330W supply has headroom for the 140W host port 
 Watch out for
 Easy to buy when a $15 USB Ethernet adapter would have done 
 Larger supply than the TS5 
 Fanless claim is the TS5's, not something to assume if you cram every port 
 Important Considerations
 • $100 more than the TS5. Skip it if 2.5GbE is enough. 
 • Still one host cable. A bad cable undoes the 10GbE port. 
 • Downstream displays on a Mac will not match every Windows triple-4K claim. 
 Disclosure: This post contains affiliate links. We may earn a commission if you purchase through these links at no additional cost to you.
 A ten-minute check after it arrives
 Plug in the dock’s own cable, not one from a drawer.
 Open System Information, Thunderbolt/USB4, and confirm the dock enumerates at 80Gb/s rather than as a USB device.
 Start a compile or an Xcode build and watch the battery icon. On a 16-inch it should climb, or at least hold, on the 140W contract. If it falls, you are on a weaker cable or a weaker port.
 Run a copy to the NAS and look at the throughput. About 280 MB/s means you got 2.5GbE. About 1 GB/s means you got 10GbE. About 110 MB/s means a 1GbE link snuck in, often the switch on the other end.
 Does a 14-inch MacBook Pro need a 140W dock? No. Apple’s fast-charge sheet treats 96W as enough for the 14-inch. A 140W dock still works, and it does not push 140W into a laptop that will not take it. Buy 140W so the same dock still makes sense if the next machine is a 16-inch.
 Can I keep using MagSafe? Yes. You can charge on MagSafe and use the dock for displays and USB. You then have two cables, which is the setup the dock was meant to retire. I would pick one. The Thunderbolt cable is the one that also carries the displays.
 Will the Anker run my Linux laptop too? Anker does not support that combination. The writeup is in the TS5 vs Anker comparison . If the second machine is Linux or an older Windows Thunderbolt laptop, buy the TS5 or the TS5 Plus.
 What I would buy
 TS5, after I confirm the laptop is M4 Pro, M4 Max, or a later Pro/Max. On a plain M4 or a 2021-2023 MacBook Pro I would buy it only if the next laptop is already on the shopping list. TS5 Plus if a 10GbE NAS is the disk I edit from. iVANKY only on a Max chip, with enough monitors to use the extra screens, and only Macs on that desk. I would not buy the Anker to save money at $399.99. I would buy it because I wanted the cube and I had checked the HDMI-or-DisplayPort port with my own eyes.

Best MacBook Pro Docks and Chargers in 2026 (PROLED XDR) 
 Skip to content 
 The best MacBook Pro docks, hubs and chargers for the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display fill the gaps its ports leave, since three Thunderbolt 5 ports, HDMI, an SDXC slot and MagSafe 3 are already built in. A dock adds Ethernet, USB-A ports and extra displays, and a Thunderbolt 5 dock can also charge the laptop at up to 140W.
 The base 14-inch model ships with a 70W adapter and needs a 96W adapter to reach 50 percent in 30 minutes , and the 16-inch needs 140W. Choose a Thunderbolt 5 dock with 140W host charging for a one-cable desk, a Thunderbolt 4 hub for ports alone, or an Apple adapter for the battery.
 iThinkDifferent may earn a commission from purchases made through links in this article. 
 Product Price Discount Why we picked it Buy 
 Anker Prime TB5 Docking Station 
 $349.99 $399.99 13% OFF Fan-cooled dock 140W host charging with two Thunderbolt 5 downstream ports. Check on Amazon 
 Anker 140W Max 4-Port GaN Charger 
 $79.99 $89.99 11% OFF Four ports One 140W USB-C port with a color display. Check on Amazon 
 Apple 96W USB-C Power Adapter 
 $73.73 Current price 14-inch fast charge 96W with a MagSafe 3 or USB-C cable. Check on Amazon 
 Apple 140W USB-C Power Adapter 
 $99 Current price 16-inch fast charge 140W with a MagSafe 3 or USB-C cable. Check on Amazon 
 CalDigit TS5 Plus Thunderbolt 5 Dock 
 $499.99 Current price 10Gb Ethernet 20 ports with 140W host charging. Check on Amazon 
 Plugable Thunderbolt 5 Dock 
 $349.95 Current price Dual HDMI 2.1 16-in-1 with 140W laptop charging. Check on Amazon 
 Satechi Thunderbolt 5 CubeDock 
 $399.99 Current price Built-in SSD bay M.2 NVMe enclosure with 140W charging. Check on Amazon 
 Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Slim Hub Pro 
 $199.99 Current price Thunderbolt 4 hub Slim hub that daisy-chains six devices. Check on Amazon 
 Base 14-Inch MacBook Pro Needs 96W to Fast Charge
 Fast charging to 50 percent in 30 minutes needs a 96W or higher USB-C source on the 14-inch MacBook Pro and 140W or higher on the 16-inch. The 14-inch model with the 15-core M5 Pro ships with a 70W adapter, so it needs a separate 96W adapter, while the 18-core M5 Pro and M5 Max configurations include 96W and the 16-inch includes 140W.
 A dock changes the same math, because the wattage it passes to the laptop is the wattage the MacBook Pro charges at. A dock with 96W or more of host charging clears the 14-inch threshold, and the 16-inch needs a dock rated for 140W.
 Apple 96W Adapter Covers the 14-Inch Fast-Charge Threshold
 The Apple 96W USB-C Power Adapter is the charger that fixes the base 14-inch model, which ships with a 70W adapter that falls short of the 96W fast-charge threshold. Apple recommends pairing it with a USB-C to MagSafe 3 Cable or USB-C Charge Cable for up to 50 percent in around 30 minutes.
 The 18-core M5 Pro and M5 Max configurations already include a 96W adapter, so on those models this is a second one for a desk or a bag. The cable is sold separately, and the 16-inch model needs the 140W adapter instead.
 Buy on Amazon · $73.73 
 Apple 140W Adapter Is the 16-Inch Fast-Charge Match
 The Apple 140W USB-C Power Adapter is the one that meets the 16-inch MacBook Pro’s fast-charge requirement of 140W or higher. Apple recommends a USB-C to MagSafe 3 Cable or USB-C Charge Cable with it for 50 percent in around 30 minutes.
 The 16-inch model already includes a 140W adapter, so this is a second one for a desk or a bag. The 14-inch model can use it as well, and the charging cable is sold separately.
 Buy on Amazon · $99 
 Anker 140W Max Charger Reaches 140W on One Port
 The Anker 140W Max 4-Port GaN Charger has three USB-C ports and one USB-A port, and each of its two main USB-C ports reaches 140W only when it is the only port in use. Two laptops split the power at 70W each.
 A laptop and a phone together still get 100W for the laptop, which clears the 14-inch threshold but not the 16-inch one, so keep the other ports empty for a 16-inch MacBook Pro. A color display shows charging status and temperature, and a 5 ft 240W USB-C to USB-C cable and an 18-month warranty come with it.
 Buy on Amazon · $79.99 $89.99 with Prime 
 Anker Prime TB5 Dock Has 14 Ports and Active Cooling
 The Anker Prime TB5 Docking Station is fan-cooled like the Satechi CubeDock but spends its ports on connections instead of an SSD bay, with a Thunderbolt 5 upstream port at up to 140W and two Thunderbolt 5 downstream ports. It also has two front USB-C ports, three USB-A ports, SD and TF readers and an audio jack.
 It has a single HDMI 2.1 or DisplayPort 2.1 output, so a second display goes through a downstream Thunderbolt 5 port on Pro and Max chips. A 3.3 ft Thunderbolt 5 cable and a 24-month warranty are in the box. The two front USB-C ports share 45W, and Ethernet is 2.5Gbps where the CalDigit TS5 Plus has 10Gb.
 Buy on Amazon · $349.99 $399.99 with Prime 
 CalDigit TS5 Plus Adds 10Gb Ethernet and 20 Ports
 The CalDigit TS5 Plus is the only dock here with 10Gb Ethernet, and its 20 ports are the most in this roundup. Three are Thunderbolt 5, ten are USB-A or USB-C at 10Gb/s, and the rest cover DisplayPort 2.1, SD 4.0 and microSD 4.0 UHS-II readers and three audio ports.
 The host port delivers up to 140W, enough for the 16-inch MacBook Pro, and a 330W supply keeps that power available as devices are added. Dual 6K 60Hz displays work on most Macs, three displays on M5 Pro and M5 Max and four on M5 Max. Dual USB controllers keep busy front and rear drives from sharing one 10Gb/s lane.
 Buy on Amazon · $499.99 
 Plugable Thunderbolt 5 Dock Adds Dual HDMI 2.1
 The Plugable Thunderbolt 5 Dock is built around two native HDMI 2.1 ports, which drive dual 8K 60Hz displays on M5 Max and M4 Max Macs and dual 6K 60Hz or 4K 144Hz on most other recent chips. Its 16 ports include six USB-C ports, two of them on the front at up to 30W each, plus 2.5GbE and 140W laptop charging.
 Every Pro and Max chip supports both displays at once. It is fanless and needs macOS 13 or later, and its Ethernet tops out at 2.5Gb where the CalDigit TS5 Plus has 10Gb.
 Buy on Amazon · $349.95 
 Satechi Thunderbolt 5 CubeDock Houses an SSD
 The Satechi Thunderbolt 5 CubeDock is the dock with a built-in SSD bay, an M.2 NVMe enclosure for drives up to 8TB that reads at up to 6000MB/s depending on the SSD. The SSD is not included, the bay takes M.2 NVMe drives only, and Satechi supports single-sided drives only.
 It adds 140W host charging, UHS-II SD and microSD readers and 2.5Gb Ethernet, with a fan that runs at 20 to 40 dB(A). Dual 6K 60Hz displays work on macOS.
 Buy on Amazon · $399.99 
 Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Slim Hub Pro Daisy-Chains Six Devices
 The Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Slim Hub Pro is the only Thunderbolt 4 hub here, with a host port, three downstream Thunderbolt 4 ports at 40Gbps and one 10Gbps USB-A port. It daisy-chains up to six devices and supports dual 4K 60Hz or a single 8K 30Hz display.
 Host charging stays below the 140W the 16-inch needs for fast charging. It has no card reader or Ethernet port, and the MacBook Pro’s built-in SDXC slot covers the card reader. A 150W power supply and a Thunderbolt 4 cable come in the box.
 Buy on Amazon · $199.99 
 What to Check in a MacBook Pro Dock or Hub
 Display limits depend on the chip, with the CalDigit TS5 Plus reaching three displays on M5 Pro and M5 Max and four on M5 Max. Thunderbolt 5 runs at 80Gb/s each way and boosts to 120Gb/s for displays, against 40Gbps on the Thunderbolt 4 hub.
 The MacBook Pro already has HDMI and an SDXC slot, so a dock earns its place with Ethernet, extra USB-A ports and more displays.
 My Pick Is the CalDigit TS5 Plus Dock
 The CalDigit TS5 Plus is the dock I would put on my desk, because it passes 140W to the host and adds 10Gb Ethernet and a dual-controller USB layout. The Plugable is the one for dual HDMI monitors, the Anker Prime TB5 is the fan-cooled port dock, and the Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Slim Hub Pro is the slim Thunderbolt 4 option. On the charger side, the base 14-inch buyer should add the Apple 96W adapter first.
 Questions About MacBook Pro Docks and Chargers
 Does the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display need a dock?
 Not for the basics, because it has three Thunderbolt 5 ports , HDMI, an SDXC slot, MagSafe 3 and a headphone jack. A dock mainly adds Ethernet, USB-A ports and extra displays.
 Which adapter does the 14-inch MacBook Pro need to fast charge?
 The 14-inch model needs a 96W or higher USB-C power source. The base configuration with the 15-core M5 Pro ships with 70W, so it needs a separate 96W adapter.
 Can a Thunderbolt 4 hub fast charge the 16-inch MacBook Pro?
 Not at the quoted speed. The 16-inch needs 140W or higher for 50 percent in 30 minutes, and the Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Slim Hub Pro stays below that.
 Does the 16-inch MacBook Pro include a charger?
 Yes. The 16-inch model includes a 140W adapter, and the 14-inch with the 18-core M5 Pro or M5 Max includes a 96W adapter.
